pathSubtitle: Practice the language of job interviews — from first impressions to tough questions and salary negotiation.

lessons.title: First Impressions
lessons.situation: You arrive for a job interview at a small company. The HR assistant meets you at the door.

dialogue.speaker: HR Assistant
dialogue.text: Good morning! Welcome. Please come in.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.text: Good morning. Thank you. My name is Sam. I have an interview at ten.

dialogue.speaker: HR Assistant
dialogue.text: Yes, of course. Please take a seat. Can I get you some water?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.text: Yes, please. Thank you very much.

dialogue.speaker: HR Assistant
dialogue.text: The interviewer will be with you in a few minutes.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.text: No problem. I will wait here.

words.definition: a meeting where someone asks you questions for a job
words.example: I have a job interview on Monday.

words.definition: to greet someone who has arrived
words.example: Welcome to our office!

words.definition: to sit down
words.example: Please take a seat and wait.

words.definition: the person who asks the questions in an interview
words.example: The interviewer smiled and shook my hand.

words.definition: to stay in one place until something happens
words.example: Please wait outside the room.

lessons.title: Tell Me About Yourself
lessons.situation: The interviewer begins the interview with the most common opening question.

dialogue.speaker: Interviewer
dialogue.text: So, tell me a little about yourself.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.text: Of course. I studied Business Management at university and graduated two years ago. Since then, I have been working as a sales assistant at a retail company.

dialogue.speaker: Interviewer
dialogue.text: And what made you apply for this position?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.text: I want to work in a bigger team and take on more responsibility. I feel this role is the right next step for my career.

dialogue.speaker: Interviewer
dialogue.text: That's great. What would you say is your greatest strength?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.text: I am very organized and I work well under pressure. My manager often gives me urgent tasks because she knows I will finish them on time.

words.definition: to make a formal request for a job or course
words.example: I applied for three jobs last week.

words.definition: a job or role in a company
words.example: She is applying for the manager position.

words.definition: a duty or task you are in charge of
words.example: I want more responsibility in my next job.

words.definition: something you are very good at
words.example: My main strength is communication.

words.definition: in a stressful situation with tight deadlines
words.example: I work well under pressure.

lessons.title: Handling Tough Questions
lessons.situation: The interview continues with more challenging questions about weaknesses and past difficulties.

dialogue.speaker: Interviewer
dialogue.text: Can you tell me about a time you made a mistake at work?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.text: Yes. Last year, I sent a report to the wrong client by mistake. I realized immediately and told my manager. We contacted the client, apologized, and sent the correct report within an hour.

dialogue.speaker: Interviewer
dialogue.text: How did your manager react?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.text: She was not happy at first, but she appreciated that I was honest and acted quickly to fix it.

dialogue.speaker: Interviewer
dialogue.text: And what is your greatest weakness?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.text: I sometimes find it difficult to delegate tasks because I like to make sure everything is done correctly. I am working on trusting my colleagues more.

words.definition: something done incorrectly or wrongly
words.example: Everyone makes mistakes — what matters is how you fix them.

words.definition: to say sorry for something you did wrong
words.example: I apologized to the client immediately.

words.definition: to recognize and value something
words.example: She appreciated my honesty.

words.definition: to give a task to someone else to do
words.example: A good manager knows how to delegate.

words.definition: something you are not as good at
words.example: My weakness is public speaking, but I am improving.

lessons.title: Salary Negotiation
lessons.situation: The interview is going well. The conversation turns to compensation.

dialogue.speaker: Interviewer
dialogue.text: We'd like to move forward with you. Before we do, can you share your salary expectations?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.text: Thank you — I'm very pleased to hear that. Based on my research and my four years of experience, I was hoping for something in the range of $55,000 to $60,000.

dialogue.speaker: Interviewer
dialogue.text: That's slightly above what we had budgeted. We were thinking closer to $50,000 to start.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.text: I understand. Could you tell me more about the full package? I'd like to consider benefits, performance reviews, and any professional development opportunities.

dialogue.speaker: Interviewer
dialogue.text: We offer annual reviews with performance bonuses, twenty-five days of holiday, and a training budget of $1,000 per year.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.text: That sounds like a strong package. I'm open to discussing the base salary further if there's some flexibility.

words.definition: the amount of pay you hope to receive
words.example: What are your salary expectations for this role?

words.definition: planned a specific amount of money for something
words.example: We budgeted $50,000 for this position.

words.definition: the total set of pay and benefits offered
words.example: The full package includes salary, bonus, and health insurance.

words.definition: extra pay given for good work results
words.example: She received a performance bonus at the end of the year.

words.definition: willingness to change or adapt
words.example: Is there flexibility on the start date?

lessons.title: Senior-Level Strategic Interview
lessons.situation: A final-round interview for a senior management role. The questions are strategic and demanding.

dialogue.speaker: Director
dialogue.text: We're looking for someone who can drive transformation across departments. Can you walk me through how you've led change in a previous role?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.text: Certainly. In my last position, I was tasked with overhauling the customer service function — it had a backlog of unresolved cases and poor satisfaction scores. I began by conducting a root-cause analysis, identified three systemic bottlenecks, and proposed a restructuring plan to the board.

dialogue.speaker: Director
dialogue.text: How did you manage resistance from the existing team?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.text: That was the most challenging part. I prioritised one-to-one conversations early on to understand concerns, framed the changes around shared goals rather than top-down mandates, and ensured the team had visibility into milestones and outcomes throughout.

dialogue.speaker: Director
dialogue.text: And what was the result?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.text: Within six months, case resolution time fell by 40% and customer satisfaction scores rose from 58% to 81%. The restructuring became a model that was adopted by two other departments.

words.definition: a fundamental and thorough change in form or character
words.example: The new CEO led a complete transformation of the company.

words.definition: a method of identifying the original cause of a problem
words.example: We carried out a root-cause analysis before proposing any solutions.

words.definition: a point of congestion that slows down a process
words.example: The approval process was a major bottleneck.

words.definition: an official instruction or authority to act
words.example: The board gave him a clear mandate to cut costs.

words.definition: an important point in the progress of a project
words.example: We hit every milestone on schedule.
